opening.headline: Understand the principles of supervised fine tuning, which teaches model behavior through examples of input and correct output, and which problems it is appropriate for.
body: Let's say you have a function that converts customer inquiries into a set JSON, but no matter how much you refine the instructions and examples, fields are sometimes missing or the wording is different. However, if you already have accumulated inputs and correct outputs, you can directly teach the model's behavior using those records.

In this class, we will look at supervised fine tuning, or SFT, what data it learns and how the format is fixed. Next, we explain when 50 examples are sufficient and when they are insufficient, and even organize standards for checking data quality.

visual.alt: A side-by-side scene showing the customer inquiry input on the left, the expected JSON output in the middle, and the actual output with fields missing on the right.
labels: Payment was made twice. Please check it quickly.

paragraphs: There is a function that reads customer inquiries and returns the classification results as specified JSON. The input is ‘Payment was made twice. Please check quickly.' It's the same sentence, and the expected output is JSON with three fields: category, urgency, and summary.

However, the actual output sometimes has fields missing or the wording is different. Although I have refined the instructions and included examples, they are not followed exactly every time. This is a problem with the action axis since the information needed is already in the input.

The team has a pile of human-reviewed input and answer output over the past few months. If you have already accumulated input and output examples, you can directly teach the model's behavior using those examples. This method is supervised fine tuning (SFT).

The OpenAI documentation explains that SFT creates custom models that more reliably produce the style and content desired for a specific application. This lesson covers its principles and eligibility conditions.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: In what way is the fact that the correct answer output already exists a condition worth attempting tuning? We will explain the reasons in class.

screens.outro: Let's think about whether there are repetitive input/output patterns in your work.

screens.title: Think about repetitive input/output patterns
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit an answer, so think of your task first and then press it.

items.prompt: Do you have a job with a repetitive input/output pattern?
items.answer: Typical tasks include producing the same type of output from the same type of input, such as classifying inquiries, summarizing meeting minutes, and writing reports in a set format. These tasks are candidates for SFT because the output of the answers is easy to collect and easy to evaluate.

items.prompt: Are the baseline outputs for that task already recorded?
items.answer: If the results confirmed by humans in the past remain in the log or system, they become the starting point for learning data. The OpenAI document also advises using historical data, data created by experts, and recorded data. If there are no records, the first thing you need to do is gather baseline output.

items.prompt: Has the standard output ever been different for each person?
items.answer: If the baseline output varies from person to person, the model also learns from that discrepancy. Data Quality Checking in this lesson covers how agreement can be an upper bound on performance.

screens.outro: Now that we've organized our thoughts, let's look at the data and flow that SFT learns from.

screens.title: Principles of SFT: Learning with input-output pairs
screens.lead: Below is an example of a training data file used in SFT. One line is a training example. Check the meaning of each part with the explanation on the right.

notes.note: JSONL format. Each line contains one complete JSON structure, and the OpenAI documentation states that the file should have at least 10 lines. If the JSON is broken in the middle of a line or the lines are merged, the file will not be readable.
One example is a list of chat messages. User input is paired with the correct response the model must produce. The model is trained to reduce the difference from the correct response given the input.

Prompts and answers should be as realistic as possible about the inputs and outputs expected in real-world applications. System instructions are also formatted in the same format as those used in actual operation. If the format is different from the time of inference, the learned behavior may not appear properly.

After training, you must compare the base model and the tuned model using evaluation data that was not used for training. The OpenAI documentation advises to set aside evaluation data from the same data before starting training.

screens.outro: Now that we know what the data looks like, let's compare how the format is fixed after training.

screens.title: The process of fixing the format
screens.lead: Select the two states alternately and compare the output before and after learning. Notice what changes for the same input.

visual.alt: For the same input, three outputs of different formats are produced before learning, and three outputs of the same format are produced after learning.
labels: Learn with examples of correct answers

states.label: Before learning
states.body:
**Same input, different appearance**: If you enter the same inquiry multiple times, sometimes you will get JSON with all three fields filled out, sometimes you will get an answer with less urgency, and sometimes you will get an answer with a line explanation.

**Support with Prompts**: In this state, you have to stick to the format by including long instructions and examples in the prompt for each request. Still, the model sometimes deviates, requiring post-processing or retry.

**Nature of the problem**: It is a behavioral problem where the information is in the input and the output method is shaky. Since the correct answer is already output, it is suitable for solving through learning. As the amount of post-processed code increases, the maintenance costs also increase.

states.label: After learning
states.body:
**Same input, same shape**: As the number of correct output examples accumulates, the model follows the output structure as is. Each time the same inquiry returns a JSON with the three fields filled out.

**High-impact uses**: The OpenAI documentation explains that SFT is good for classification, nuanced translation, creating content in a specific format, and correcting failures to follow instructions. Effective tasks for Google Cloud Documents include classification, summarization, abstract Q&A, and conversation.

**Limitations**: Quality is limited by the consistency of the data. As in the example of the OpenAI document, if people only agreed 70% of the passages they extracted, it's hard for the model to get any better than that. So we first check the consistency of the examples.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the appropriate conditions, let’s use an example to determine whether the number of examples is sufficient.

screens.title: Explanation: When 50 examples are enough and when they are not enough
screens.lead: The instructor judges both cases in the same order. Select the right arrow to skip a step. Learners do not enter answers.

steps.title: Check OpenAI’s recommendations
steps.body: The OpenAI document states that the minimum number of examples that can be provided for fine tuning is 10, and that improvements are seen with 50 to 100 examples. The optimal number will vary greatly depending on your use case, so we recommend starting with 50 well-executed examples and evaluating them.

steps.title: Case A: The format is simple and the examples are consistent.
steps.body: The first case involves converting a query into JSON with three fields. The format is simple, and there are examples confirmed by the people in charge using the same standards. The types of input are also not very diverse.

steps.title: Judgment of Case A: Evaluate 50
steps.body: In this case, it is worth learning with 50 examples and then comparing the field omission rate with evaluation data. If the missing rate decreases noticeably, it is effective. Once you see improvement, at that point decide whether to stop or increase it further.

steps.title: Case B: There are many boundary cases and the inputs are varied.
steps.body: In the second case, there are dozens of categories of customer inquiries, similar categories must be distinguished from each other, and the expressions of the inquiries are very diverse. 50 examples may not be enough to cover this distribution. This is because there are few rare edge cases in the training data.

steps.title: Case B decision: Increase data but look at quality first
steps.body: The OpenAI documentation explains that you should expect a similar amount of improvement every time you double the number of training examples. If you already see some effect with 50, add more examples targeting boundary cases. The amount of improvement can be approximated compared to results learned from half-sized data.

steps.title: When there is no improvement: Check before increasing the amount.
steps.body: If you study with 50 and there is little change in the assessment, look at the task definition and prompt again before increasing the examples tenfold. The article also suggests that if 50 doesn't work, you should rethink the task or prompt before adding data. This is because the problem may not be the amount of data.

steps.title: Summary: Look at quality before quantity
steps.body: OpenAI's best practices state that, if a choice must be made, small amounts of high-quality data are usually more effective than large amounts of low-quality data. So, it is safe to first make 50 well, evaluate them, and increase them according to the results. If you follow this order, it will be clear which step was effective.

screens.outro: Lastly, let's look at the criteria for checking data quality using cards.

screens.title: Data quality check
screens.lead: The following flashcards illustrate five criteria for checking training data. When you select a card, it flips over. Select the right arrow to go to the next card.

visual.alt: Check card icon with check mark.
labels: Does the example contain all the information needed to respond?
Is the rate of rejections similar to the actual expected rate?
Is the format the same as the input during inference?
Are examples created by multiple people consistent with each other?
Check problematic examples first and then increase the amount.

cards.front: Does the example contain all the information needed to respond?
cards.back: If the correct response refers to information that is not in the input, the model can learn to invent the information. As an example in the OpenAI document, hallucinations are learned if the training data contains responses praising user characteristics that are not in the conversation. Check whether the correct answer can be derived from the input.

cards.front: Is the rate of rejections similar to the actual expected rate?
cards.back: If 60% of the training data is unable to answer, but only 5% actually should, the model is likely to overreject. The balance and diversity of data must follow the distribution of the operating environment.

cards.front: Is the format the same as the input during inference?
cards.back: All training examples must be in the format expected for inference. If there are inconsistencies such as system instructions in the training data that are not present in the operation, the behavior learned by the model may not be produced properly.

cards.front: Are examples created by multiple people consistent with each other?
cards.back: When data is created by multiple people, model performance may be limited by agreement and consistency across people. If only 70% of people agreed on the elicitation task, it's hard for your model to be any better than that. Meet the writing standards first with your writing.

cards.front: Check problematic examples first and then increase the amount.
cards.back: If your model shows problems with grammar, logic, or style, first check to see if the same problems exist in your data. If your model says something it shouldn't say, check to see if any existing examples teach it. Increasing quantity comes after checking quality.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the inspection criteria, we will organize the class on the final screen.

screens.title: SFT teaches behavior through examples of correct answers.
screens.lead: We conclude the class by answering the question posed at the beginning: why already having the correct answer output is a condition worth attempting tuning.

paragraphs: The team for the first scene had a problem with missing fields even after refining the instructions and examples. It was a behavioral problem where the information was in the input and the output method was unstable, and the output of correct answers confirmed by humans was piled up. Supervised learning teaches the model’s behavior using these input-output pairs.

There are two eligibility conditions for SFT. The task must be well defined and there must be labeled answer data. This includes tasks where the shape of the correct answer is clear, such as classification, generation of a specific format, correction of failure to follow instructions, summarization, and abstract Q&A.

The order of progress is to prepare evaluation first, prepare examples containing actual input and output in JSONL, start learning with about 50 well-made examples, and verify with evaluation data not used for learning. If it's not effective, check the quality of your task definition, prompts, and examples before increasing data.

Quality is more important than quantity. Make sure the examples have the information you need, that the proportions are similar to your environment, that the format is the same, and that there is agreement between authors. Lastly, remember that SFT is a way to change behavior. This is not a method of incorporating in-house knowledge, and such problems are solved through search. These criteria are the starting point for deciding whether or not to start SFT.

callout.label: Based on one sentence
callout.text: If you have an example output of correct answers and the problem is behavior, review the SFT, start with 50 and increase with evaluation.

checks.intro: Check for yourself by recalling the shape of the training data you just saw. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: What is the basic form of training data provided to the model in SFT?
options: Pair a prompt with the desired model output
A large amount of original text collected without correct answers
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. SFT learns pairs of prompt and answer outputs.
checks.incorrectFeedback: That form is not SFT's training data. Think back to what each line in the code example consists of.
checks.explain: SFT adjusts the weights to reduce the difference between the prompted and baseline output of the labeled dataset.

wrong.0: Preferred/non-preferred pairs are used in DPO.
wrong.3: Search fragments are for context injection and are not a form of training data.

checks.intro: Think about the flow of SFT and put them in order. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Put the SFT process in order.
items: Prepare an example containing actual input and output in JSONL.
Verify with an evaluation set that was not used for training.
If the effect is insufficient, increase data
checks.correctFeedback: The order of preparation, launch, verification, and expansion was set correctly.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is incorrect. After looking at the evaluation results, think again about increasing the data.
checks.explain: OpenAI recommends starting with 50 well-crafted examples and evaluating them. Look at the evaluation results and decide whether to increase data.

checks.intro: Check the last question, thinking about how to respond when there is no improvement as seen in the commentary. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: I studied with 50 examples, but there was little improvement in the evaluation. What should I do first?
options: Mix the evaluation set into the training data
We conclude that SFT is not effective for all tasks.
Recheck the quality of task definitions, prompts, and examples
checks.correctFeedback: That's correct. Before increasing the quantity, you should check the quality of your task definition and examples.
checks.incorrectFeedback: That response is not appropriate. If you increase the amount or obscure the verification without confirming the cause, judgment becomes difficult.
checks.explain: If 50 doesn't work, look at the task or prompt again before increasing the data. Quality is more important than quantity.

wrong.0: Increasing the amount without checking the cause may result in waste.

wrong.2: It works well for the right tasks.

glossary.def: This is a method of training a model with data given input and reference output.
This is a training example that combines a prompt and desired response.
The idea is to make the output structure look the same every time.
A file format that places one complete JSON per line. Each training example is one line.
This is data that is not used for learning but only for performance comparison.

misconceptions.fact: Quality and consistency come first. Small amounts of high-quality data are usually more effective than large amounts of low-quality data.

misconceptions.myth: SFT allows internal knowledge to be incorporated into the model.
misconceptions.fact: SFT is a way to change behavior. It is correct to input changing knowledge and private knowledge through search.
There must first be an evaluation to determine whether the tuned model is better than the base model. If you learn without evaluation, you won't know whether you are improving.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: SFT teaches behavior as a pair of input and correct output.
Suitable conditions include well-defined tasks and labeled data.
Start with 50 well-made examples, evaluate them, and increase based on results.
Data quality is more important than quantity.
